00001| --- 00002| title: Designing view transitions 00003| description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 00004| nav_title: View transitions 00005| --- 00006| 00007| In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 00008| 00009| Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 00010| 00011| React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 00012| 00013| This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 00014| 00015| ## Add view transitions with an agent 00016| 00017| The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 00018| 00019| Install the skill: 00020| 00021| ```bash filename="Terminal" 00022| npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 00023| ``` 00024| 00025| Then prompt the agent with something like: 00026| 00027| ```prompt 00028| Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 00029| ``` 00030| 00031| Or prompt for a specific transition, such as: 00032| 00033| - Morphing a thumbnail into a hero image 00034| - Sliding between routes forward and back 00035| - Crossfading content within the same route 00036| 00037| To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 00038| 00039| ## Example 00040| 00041| As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 00042| 00043| We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 00044| 00045| You can find the resources used in this example here: 00046| 00047| - ---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

Install the skill:

/**
 * OpenCode in-sandbox runner.
 *
 * This file is shipped INTO the sandbox by the orchestrator and executed there as
 * `node __agent_eval__/run.mjs '<AgentRunInput JSON>'`. It is intentionally
 * ZERO-DEPENDENCY (only `node:*` builtins) because the sandbox only has the
 * fixture's own deps + the installed `opencode` CLI — it cannot import anything
 * from the @vercel/agent-eval package.
 *
 * Dual mode:
 *   - runnable: invoked directly → reads argv, runs the agent, writes the result
 *     file + prints a status line, exits 0.
 *   - importable: `import { runAgent } from './run.mjs'` → returns a RunnerResult
 *     (no file write, no exit). This is what a future in-sandbox judge reuses.
 *
 * The pure helpers below are exported (not just `runAgent`) so they can be
 * unit-tested directly — the same code the sandbox runs (see opencode.test.ts).
 */

part.text:
Build and typecheck pass. Changes:

- **Shared element morph** — grid thumbnails (`app/ProductGrid.tsx:15`) and the detail hero (`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx:58`) are wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`, so the image scales/repositions between pages; `via-blur` mid-flight keyframe at 400ms in `app/globals.css:135`.
- **Directional slides** — grid links use `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`, the back link `nav-back`; both pages are wrapped in a `ViewTransition` mapping those types to `nav-forward`/`nav-back` slide+fade animations (60px offset).
- **Suspense reveals** — skeletons wrapped in `exit="slide-down"`, real content in `enter="slide-up"` (both `default="none"` so they only fire on reveal).
- **Reduced motion** — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` zeroes all view-transition durations/delays and disables the skeleton pulse (`app/globals.css:227`); `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` keeps the page clickable mid-transition.
